items.prose: A pricing library needs Python 3.11 or newer. Four machines report their versions.
items.question: Which machine can run it?

options.why: You read 3.9 as a decimal, bigger than 3.11. Its minor number, 9, is below 11.
You let the patch, 15, carry it. The minor number, 10, is below 11, so the patch never counts.
You let the patch, 19, carry it. The minor number, 8, decides first.

feedback.correct: Only C has minor 11 or more.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the minor numbers as whole numbers.

explain.text: All four have major 3, so the minor numbers decide: 9, 10, 11 and 8. Only C reaches 11. Patch numbers matter only when the minor numbers tie.

items.prose: `hi.py` holds one line, `print("hi")`, saved from VS Code with Enter pressed at the end.
items.question: How many bytes is the file?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count every character, quotes and newline included.

byKey.no-newline: You counted the visible characters. Pressing Enter saved a newline as well.
byKey.no-quotes: You skipped two characters. The quotes are bytes too, and so is the newline.

explain.text: `print("hi")` is p, r, i, n, t, the bracket, a quote, h, i, a quote and a bracket: 11 characters. The newline makes 12 bytes. A plain-text file is exactly its characters.

items.prose: Ana's PATH is `/opt/homebrew/bin:/usr/bin:/bin`. Two folders hold a `git`.
items.question: What does `git --version` report?

options.why: You picked the system copy. The search starts at the left of the PATH and stops at `/opt/homebrew/bin`.
You expected the shell to object. It stops at the first match and never sees the second.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Walk the PATH from the left.

explain.text: The shell opens `/opt/homebrew/bin` first and finds `git` there. It runs that copy, 2.47.1, and stops. `which git` would confirm it.

items.prose:
A script holds three lines:

```python
price = 50.00
price = price * 2
print(price - 25)
```
items.question: What number does it print?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Track `price` line by line.

byKey.old: You used the first price, 50. Line 2 replaced it with 100 before the print.
byKey.no-sub: You stopped at the new price. Line 3 prints `price - 25`.

explain.text: Line 1 sets 50.00. Line 2 replaces it with 100.0. Line 3 prints 100.0 − 25 = 75.0.

items.prose: VS Code has the folder `/Users/ana/research` open. Its built-in terminal prints `python3: can't open file '/Users/ana/research/src/signal.py'` after Ana types `python3 src/signal.py`. Her script is `/Users/ana/research/signal.py`.
items.question: Which command runs the script from that terminal?

options.why: You started from her home folder. The terminal is already in `research`, so that path means `research/research/signal.py`.
You left out `python3`. The shell would search the PATH for a program called `signal.py`.

feedback.correct: The file sits directly in the terminal's folder.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Join the terminal's folder to the name you type.

explain.text: The terminal is in `/Users/ana/research`, and the file is right there. So the name alone, `signal.py`, finds it. There is no `src` folder in the way.

items.prose: At 10:00 Ana installs Python 3.12, and the installer adds `/opt/python/bin` to the front of her PATH settings. Two windows give different answers.
items.question: Why does the 9:00 window report 3.9.6?

options.text: It still has its 9:00 PATH, without `/opt/python/bin`

options.why: You blamed the install. The 10:05 window runs 3.12.4, so the install worked.

options.text: Two versions cannot live on one machine
options.why: They can, side by side. Which one runs depends only on the PATH the window searches.

feedback.correct: Old window, old PATH, older Python found first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about when each window read its PATH.

explain.text: Each window copies the PATH when it opens. The 9:00 copy has no `/opt/python/bin`, so the search finds the Mac's 3.9.6 in `/usr/bin`. Close it and open a new one.

items.prose:
A script stops with this message:

```text
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/Users/ana/first-script/gain.py", line 4, in <module>
    gain = (close - start) / start
            ~~~~~~^~~~~~~
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for -: 'float' and 'str'
```

Line 1 of `gain.py` reads `start = "250.00"`.
items.question: What should Ana change?

options.text: Line 1, so that `start` holds the number 250.00, without quotes

options.why: You fixed the line the message names. The formula is right; line 1 made `start` text.
Python subtracts numbers happily. It cannot take text away from a number.

feedback.correct: The cause is the quotes, on line 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask where the text came from.

explain.text: The last line says what: a number minus text. The `File` line says where: line 4. The quotes on line 1 made `start` text, so that is the line to fix.

items.prose: One of Ana's backtests needs pandas 1.5 and another needs pandas 2.2. Both run on the same Python.
items.question: What should she make in each project?

options.text: A copy of the project folder
options.why: You copied the code. The clash is in the libraries, which live with Python, not with the code.

options.text: Nothing: pip keeps both versions in one folder
options.why: You expected pip to keep both. One Python folder holds one pandas, so the second install replaces the first.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each project needs its own place for libraries.

explain.text: A virtual environment is a private Python folder for one project. With it activated, pip installs there only. Two projects, two folders, two versions.

items.prose: A 600-word script. Ana typed 30 words a minute looking at the keys; after keybr practice she types 50 without looking.
items.question: How many minutes does she save on the script?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find both times, then subtract.

byKey.speeds: You found the old time, or subtracted the speeds. Both give 20; the saving is 20 − 12.
byKey.new: You gave the new time. The question asks how much she saves.

explain.text: 600 ÷ 30 = 20 minutes, and 600 ÷ 50 = 12 minutes. She saves 8 minutes, and keeps her eyes on the screen.
